subject: Physics
subtopic: Universal gravitation, free fall and orbital motion
axis_note: ladder_position is a curriculum coordinate. It is never a learner estimate; teaching depth is intrinsic, while practice percentages only route support.

must_contain: Two-body diagrams with equal-and-opposite direction arrows on the same joining line.
A comparison where the identities of the two bodies are swapped without changing the interaction pair.

controlled_variation.vary: which body is labelled A and which B
controlled_variation.hold: the two masses and their separation
controlled_variation.notice: the force arrows reverse ownership but remain collinear and paired

controlled_variation.vary: the relative position of the pair in the page
controlled_variation.notice: rotating the picture rotates both arrows without changing their magnitudes

rungs.aha: For fixed masses, gravitational-force magnitude falls with the square of centre-to-centre distance, while doubling either mass doubles the magnitude.
learner_owns: Gravitational interaction is mutual and points along the line joining the two bodies.
Can compare products and square ratios.
must_contain: The centre-to-centre distance, not surface gap, identified before substitution.
A ratio comparison that changes distance while masses are held fixed, then changes one mass while distance is held fixed.

misconception.wrong_idea: Doubling the separation halves the gravitational force.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: Two identical pairs are separated by r and 2r. Is the second force half, one quarter, or unchanged?
misconception.repair: Use the inverse square on distance: a factor of two in separation produces a factor of four in the denominator.

rungs.closure: Predict the force-factor change for one mass doubled and separation tripled, and justify the two factors separately.

controlled_variation.notice: equal steps in distance do not produce equal steps in force; the square controls the change

engineering_dependencies.reason: Inverse-square force and mass dependence need gate ownership.
Quantitative force-ratio work needs an implemented validator.

rungs.aha: The gravitational acceleration produced by a source mass is independent of the falling object's mass because the same test mass appears in both gravitational force and inertia.
learner_owns: The inverse-square force law can be used with centre-to-centre distance.
Can use F=ma as a relation between net force and acceleration.
must_contain: The test mass shown once in the gravitational force and once in F=ma before cancellation.
A same-location comparison of two different falling masses.

misconception.wrong_idea: A heavier object has a larger gravitational force, so it must have a larger free-fall acceleration.
misconception.diagnostic_prompt: At the same location, a 10 kg object feels twice the gravitational force of a 5 kg object. Does it accelerate twice as fast?
misconception.repair: Carry the mass into F=ma; both force and inertia scale by the same factor, so the acceleration does not.

rungs.closure: Given two different test masses at the same radius from a planet, predict and compare their accelerations without using numerical values.

controlled_variation.notice: force changes with test mass but acceleration does not

engineering_dependencies.reason: The cancellation of test mass into gravitational acceleration needs gate ownership.

must_contain: The zero of gravitational potential energy stated explicitly as infinite separation.
A comparison between bound circular motion and the minimum-energy escape case at the same radius.

controlled_variation.hold: source mass, test mass, and chosen potential-energy zero
controlled_variation.notice: kinetic energy changes while the gravitational potential term is unchanged

controlled_variation.vary: from a circular-orbit case to a just-escape case
controlled_variation.hold: the same launch radius and central mass
controlled_variation.notice: the escape case requires a higher kinetic contribution because its limiting total energy is zero

must_contain: An orbital-plane drawing with position and momentum as in-plane polar vectors and angular momentum shown as an axial vector normal to the plane.
The same orbit shown from the opposite face so the axial direction convention must be applied rather than guessed from clockwise/counter-clockwise words alone.

controlled_variation.vary: the satellite's position around the orbit
controlled_variation.hold: central force directed through the same origin
controlled_variation.notice: the torque arm and force stay collinear, so external torque about the centre remains zero

controlled_variation.vary: the viewing side of the orbital plane
controlled_variation.hold: the physical orbit and sense of motion
controlled_variation.notice: the axial-vector arrow appears reversed to the viewer, while the physical angular-momentum direction is unchanged

family.invariant_demand: Identify the interacting masses and centre-to-centre radius, choose the gravitational relation that fits the requested quantity, preserve vector direction or energy sign, and check the result against scaling or conservation.
family.difficult_move: Deciding which gravitational model is being asked for—force, local acceleration, energy, or orbital angular momentum—before inserting numbers.
family.independent_check: Change one controlling quantity mentally: inverse-square results must scale with radius as expected, while conservation results must preserve their stated invariant.

support_ladder.handed_over: The relevant model is named and the controlling radius or energy reference is identified; the learner still executes the relation and the check.
The interacting bodies and centre-to-centre radius are marked; the learner chooses the model and completes the check.
Only the physical situation and requested quantity are given.

transfer.changed_demand: A satellite experiences an additional tangential thrust: decide whether angular momentum about the planet is still conserved.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: whether the added force produces a non-zero external torque about the chosen centre

transfer.changed_demand: A force-versus-radius graph replaces the inverse-square formula; infer how gravitational force scales when radius changes.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: the inverse-square exponent represented by the graph

transfer.changed_demand: From a launch at the planet surface, determine whether a stated speed gives a bound orbit, escape, or an impossible energy classification.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: the total-energy threshold that separates bound motion from escape

transfer.changed_demand: Two small asteroids of comparable mass attract each other in deep space rather than a small object falling toward a planet.
transfer.information_not_handed_over: that the same mutual inverse-square interaction applies symmetrically when neither body is an obvious fixed source
